body_text:
The Chain Rule. Let $U, V \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be open intervals.
If $f : U \to V$ is differentiable at $x_0 \in U$ and $g : V \to \mathbb{R}$
is differentiable at $f(x_0) \in V$, then the composite function $g \circ f$
is differentiable at $x_0$, with derivative given by:
$$ (g \circ f)'(x_0) = g'(f(x_0)) \cdot f'(x_0). $$

*Proof (Carathéodory's Formulation)*: Differentiability of $g$ at $y_0 = f(x_0)$
is equivalent to the existence of a function $\psi : V \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous
at $y_0$ such that $g(y) - g(y_0) = \psi(y)(y - y_0)$, with $\psi(y_0) = g'(y_0)$.
Similarly, $f(x) - f(x_0) = \phi(x)(x - x_0)$ with $\phi$ continuous at $x_0$ and $\phi(x_0) = f'(x_0)$.
Substituting $y = f(x)$ gives:
$$ (g \circ f)(x) - (g \circ f)(x_0) = \psi(f(x))(f(x) - f(x_0)) = [\psi(f(x)) \cdot \phi(x)](x - x_0). $$
Since $f$ is continuous at $x_0$ and $\psi$ is continuous at $f(x_0)$, the product
$\psi(f(x)) \cdot \phi(x)$ is continuous at $x_0$.
Taking the limit as $x \to x_0$ yields $(g \circ f)'(x_0) = \psi(f(x_0)) \cdot \phi(x_0) = g'(f(x_0)) f'(x_0)$.
